column1: In SQL Server, a common table expression (CTE) defines a {{c1::named result set}} from a query.
column2:
The name can serve as a table source in the following query, even though no separate table is created.
Review source

column1: A SQL Server CTE definition is available to {{c1::one following statement}}.
column2:
Two references inside one SELECT are allowed. A second SELECT needs a new definition or a separately stored result.
Review source

column1: {{c1::WITH}} N AS (SELECT 1 AS n) SELECT n FROM N; defines and uses a SQL Server CTE.
column2:
The parenthesized SELECT defines N. SELECT n FROM N consumes the definition immediately.
Review source

column1: Before a SQL Server CTE, terminate the preceding statement in the same batch with {{c1::a semicolon}}.
column2:
The semicolon belongs to the statement before WITH. It is not part of the CTE name or definition.
Review source

column1: Separate multiple SQL Server CTE definitions in one WITH clause with {{c1::commas}}.
column2:
The comma marks the boundary between two named queries. Do not start a second WITH at that boundary.
Review source

column1: A SQL Server CTE can reference a different CTE defined {{c1::earlier in the same WITH clause}}.
column2:
Order the definitions so a prerequisite appears before its consumer. Only recursion permits a definition to reference itself.
Review source

column1: To use one SQL Server CTE in both inputs of a self-join, assign its references {{c1::different aliases}}.
column2:
For example, alias one reference e and the other m when matching employees to managers.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, CTE results are {{c1::not materialized}} automatically for reuse.
column2:
Do not treat a CTE as a cache. Inspect the plan or store the result separately if repeated work matters.
Review source

column1: A SQL Server CTE that references itself to traverse a hierarchy is a {{c1::recursive CTE}}.
column2:
Each step takes rows from the last step and follows another level of the relationship.
Review source

column1: In a recursive SQL Server CTE, the {{c1::anchor member}} supplies the initial rows.
column2:
The anchor produces the root or other starting rows without using the recursive result.
Review source

column1: A SQL Server CTE's recursive member uses rows from {{c1::the immediately preceding iteration}}.
column2:
If the anchor returns a manager and the first step returns employees, the next step starts with those employees.
Review source

column1: In a SQL Server recursive CTE, {{c1::UNION ALL}} connects the last anchor member to the first recursive member.
column2:
The operator combines the anchor and recursive outputs without removing repeated rows.
Review source

column1: SQL Server CTE recursion normally stops when the recursive member {{c1::returns no rows}}.
column2:
An empty step leaves nothing for the next step to process. Make sure cycles cannot keep supplying rows.
Review source

column1: SQL Server limits a recursive CTE to {{c1::100 recursion levels}} by default.
column2:
This is a depth limit rather than a limit on the total result rows. One level can produce many rows.
Review source

column1: To limit a SQL Server recursive CTE to 200 recursion levels, use OPTION ({{c1::MAXRECURSION 200}}).
column2:
Use the hint when you know a valid hierarchy can exceed the default. It still protects against unexpectedly deep traversal.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server, OPTION (MAXRECURSION {{c1::0}}) removes the recursion limit.
column2:
Zero removes the safeguard. It does not cause the query to stop after the anchor.
Review source

column1: In a SQL Server SELECT using a recursive CTE, place OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) on {{c1::the outermost SELECT statement}}.
column2:
Set the limit on the statement using the CTE, not inside the parenthesized query.
Review source

column1: A recursive date CTE advances DateValue by one day with {{c1::DATEADD(DAY, 1, DateValue)}}.
column2:
The expression advances from one generated date to the next. The recursive filter decides when to stop generating.
Review source

column1: To retain generated CTE dates without matching orders, put the dates on the left of a {{c1::LEFT JOIN}}.
column2:
The join preserves a date even if none of the order rows satisfy the join condition.
Review source

column1: A CTE used by an UPDATE can define {{c1::the target rows to change}}.
column2:
The CTE expresses the row filter separately from the write. The UPDATE still changes the underlying table.
Review source
